title: Hagar and Ishmael in the desert (Genesis 21:9–21)
hook: sent away with bread and water, Hagar weeps; God hears the boy and opens her eyes to a well

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lot's wife looks back, and becomes a pillar of salt. Your line was face forward. What did you stop looking back at? Day forty-seven.

Isaac is born, the laughing baby. When he's weaned, Abraham throws a great feast. And at the feast, Sarah sees Ishmael, Hagar's son, Isaac's older brother, laughing, or playing, or mocking. The Hebrew word is from the same root as Isaac's name, and readers disagree about what it means here. Sarah tells Abraham: send this servant and her son away. Abraham is deeply upset, the Torah says, because of his son. God tells him to listen to Sarah, and promises that Ishmael, too, will become a nation. So early the next morning, Abraham takes bread and a skin of water, puts them on Hagar's shoulder, gives her the boy, and sends them away. Into the wilderness of Beer-sheba. Today: Ishmael, heard in the desert.
screen: `A FEAST FOR ISAAC.` → `SEND THEM AWAY.` → `BREAD AND A SKIN OF WATER.`

segments.voice: The water runs out. Hagar puts her son under a bush and walks off about a bowshot away, and sits down. In the old JPS translation: "Let me not look upon the death of the child." She lifts up her voice and weeps. Then a small detail with enormous weight: "God heard the voice of the lad." Hagar is the one weeping, but it's the boy God hears. Remember his name? Ishmael. It means God hears. His name, given by the angel before he was born, comes true in the desert. An angel calls to her: "What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is." Where he is. The rabbis built a teaching on those three words. The Talmud reads them as: God judges him as he is right now, a thirsty boy, not by anything that might come later. And then: "God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water." Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say God made a well. It says God opened her eyes. The well was there all along. She was too deep in grief to see it. A midrash draws a big lesson from this: all people are presumed blind until God opens their eyes. She fills the skin and gives the boy a drink. And the Torah adds: God was with the lad, and he grew. This chapter is the synagogue Torah reading on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, the new year. So the year's reading includes a mother weeping in the desert, and a well she couldn't see.
screen: `A BOWSHOT AWAY, WEEPING.` · `GOD HEARD THE LAD.` · `WHERE HE IS.` · `GOD OPENED HER EYES.` · then, large: `THE WELL WAS THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of something that feels like a desert right now: a dry stretch, a place where you've run out. Let yourself admit it, the way Hagar sat down and wept. Then, gently, look around it. Is there a well you haven't noticed? A friend who has offered help. A resource you forgot you had. A small thing that has been keeping you going. Don't force it. Let your eyes open slowly. If you pray, you can ask to see. The bell holds the time.
Ishmael, the boy whose name means God hears, found again in the desert when God opened his mother's eyes to a well that was there all along.
Your line: the well was there. Today, when you feel dry, stop and look for the well you haven't noticed. Day forty-seven.

fork.setup: you're Hagar. the water is gone and your son is dying of thirst. what do you do?
options: put him under a bush, sit a bowshot away, and weep.
fork.reveal: she can't bear to watch him die, and weeps. God hears the boy, and opens her eyes to a well that was already there.

original.note: Hebrew: a well. the same word as in Beer-sheba and Beer-lahai-roi.

trapdoor: what you thought: God worked a miracle and made water.
what it means: God opened Hagar's eyes. the well was there, and grief had hidden it.
what a scholar hears: Rosh Hashanah 16b reads "where he is" as judging a person by the present; Genesis Rabbah 53:14 learns that all are blind until God opens their eyes.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 21:16, 21:17 and 21:19. 'God heard the voice of the lad' (21:17a) is inside the quoted verse range.
Metzachek (21:9): meaning disputed (playing, laughing, mocking; midrash reads worse). The script says nobody agrees. Confirm.
Rosh Hashanah 16b / Rashi on 21:17: judged 'ba'asher hu sham', by present deeds. Confirm.
Genesis Rabbah 53:14: 'all are presumed blind until the Holy One opens their eyes'. Paraphrased; confirm.
Genesis 21 as the first-day Rosh Hashanah Torah reading: confirm.
Abraham's distress 'because of his son' (21:11) paraphrased.

Editor review (2026-10-01): removed 'now a teenager' (an age the text never gives; it sits awkwardly with 21:14–15); 'nobody agrees' now 'readers disagree'; Genesis Rabbah 53:14 paraphrased closer to its wording ('all are presumed blind'); the Rosh Hashanah line no longer says the year 'opens with' Hagar (the reading begins with Isaac's birth); 'God heard the voice of the lad' (21:17a) now listed in sources as quoted.
